author: Philostorgius
occasion: Philostorgius wrote a church history continuing and correcting Eusebius, from an Arian perspective, covering events down to the reign of Constantius and beyond.
argument: Philostorgius evaluates earlier Jewish and Christian historical writings, praising the first book of Maccabees while rejecting the third and giving a mixed assessment of Eusebius, whom he praises in other respects but says erred concerning piety. He traces the origin of the Arian controversy specifically to the presbyter Alexander Baucalis, who held second rank and started the cause from which the quarrel between Alexander the bishop and Arius broke out; from there, Philostorgius says, the proclamation of homoousios was contrived. He also records the death of Constantius, father of Constantine, and Constantine's succession. Following common tradition, he attributes Constantine's conversion to Christianity to his victory over Daxentius.

outline.move: Philostorgius assesses the books of Maccabees, Josephus, and Eusebius, then recounts the origin of the Arian dispute and the death of Constantine's father Constantius.

cast.name: Philostorgius
cast.who: The author, an Arian church historian.

cast.name: Jason of Cyrene
cast.who: Hellenistic Jewish historian whose five-volume work is summarized in 2 Maccabees.

cast.name: Judas Maccabeus
cast.who: Jewish leader who fought Antiochus Epiphanes.

cast.name: Antiochus Epiphanes
cast.who: Seleucid king opposed by Judas Maccabeus.

cast.name: Josephus
cast.who: Jewish historian; Philostorgius attributes the fourth book of Maccabees to him, though modern scholarship does not.

cast.name: Phlegon
cast.who: Pagan historian who briefly mentioned events concerning the Jews.

cast.name: Dion
cast.who: Pagan historian who briefly mentioned events concerning the Jews.

cast.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
cast.who: Church historian, associated with Pamphilus, whom Philostorgius praises in other respects but criticizes theologically.

cast.name: Arius
cast.who: Alexandrian presbyter whose dispute with Alexander began the Arian controversy.

cast.name: Alexander
cast.who: Bishop of Alexandria, opponent of Arius.

cast.name: Alexander Baucalis
cast.who: Alexandrian presbyter nicknamed Baucalis, distinct from Alexander the bishop; he held second rank and is said to have started the cause from which the quarrel between Alexander the bishop and Arius broke out.

cast.name: Constantius
cast.who: Father of Constantine the Great, emperor in the upper Galatias, where the Alps are.

cast.name: Constantine
cast.who: Son of Constantius, later Constantine the Great.

cast.name: Daxentius
cast.who: Rival emperor defeated by Constantine; the manuscript form is Daxentius, likely a corruption of Maxentius.

voices.speaker: Philostorgius
voices.how_marked: Main narrative voice; introduced by φησι or Ὅτι.

key_terms.sense: The doctrine that the Son is of the same substance as the Father, which Philostorgius says was contrived during the Arian dispute.
The high priesthood or episcopal office, here the votes for the bishopric that Arius allegedly lost to Alexander.
True piety or right worship, which Philostorgius claims Eusebius erred about.
The books of Maccabees, Jewish historical writings evaluated by Philostorgius.
Historical writing or inquiry, the genre Philostorgius is evaluating and composing.
Emperor or king, used for Constantius and Constantine.
The second rank or position held by Alexander Baucalis, indicating his subordinate status to the bishop.

scripture: Philostorgius refers to the books of Maccabees and the prophecies of Daniel. Cite them by their standard English names: 1 Maccabees, 2 Maccabees, 3 Maccabees, 4 Maccabees, and Daniel.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is approximate.
The identity of the addressee is not stated in the surviving text.
The precise wording of the source is damaged in several places, so some details about Phlegon, Dion, and Josephus remain uncertain.
The manuscript form Δαξεντίου is likely a corruption of Maxentius, but the identification is not certain.
The exact location of Constantius's death is uncertain; the source has a damaged place name.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He traces the origin of the Arian controversy specifically to the presbyter Alexander Baucalis, who held second rank and started the cause from which the quarrel between Alexander the bishop and Arius broke out; from there, Philostorgius says, the proclamation of homoousios was contrived.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τοῦτόν φησιν τὴν δευτέραν τάξιν μετ᾽ ἔχοντα ἄρξαι τῆς αἰτίας ἐξ ἧς ἡ διαφορὰ Ἀλεξάνδρῳ τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ καὶ Ἀρείῳ συνερράγη. καὶ τὴν τοῦ ὁμοουσίου ἀνακήρυξιν ἐκεῖθεν ἐπιτεχνασθῆναι
_unresolved_facts.fix: Philostorgius traces the origin of the Arian controversy to the presbyter Alexander Baucalis, who held second rank and started the cause from which the quarrel between Alexander the bishop and Arius broke out; and from there, he says, the proclamation of homoousios was contrived. Note: The source says ἐκεῖθεν ἐπιτεχνασθῆναι ('was contrived from there'), but does not explicitly say Philostorgius himself endorsed this view as true—he reports it as part of his narrative.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Following common tradition, he attributes Constantine's conversion to Christianity to his victory over Daxentius.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τοῖς ἄλλοις ἐσυμφθεγγόμενος αἰτίαν γενέσθαι ἀναγράφει τὴν κατὰ Δαξεντίου νίκην
_unresolved_facts.fix: Following common tradition, he records that the victory over Daxentius became the cause of Constantine's conversion to Christianity. Note: The source says τοῖς ἄλλοις ἐσυμφθεγγόμενος ('agreeing with others/singing the same song as others'), indicating Philostorgius follows common tradition, but the text is damaged and cuts off at ἣν.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Alexander Baucalis ... distinct from Alexander the bishop; he held second rank and is said to have started the cause from which the quarrel between Alexander the bishop and Arius broke out
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἀλέξανδρόν τινα πρεσβύτερον Βαύκαλιν ἐπονομαζόμενον ... τοῦτόν φησιν τὴν δευτέραν τάξιν μετ᾽ ἔχοντα ἄρξαι τῆς αἰτίας ἐξ ἧς ἡ διαφορὰ Ἀλεξάνδρῳ τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ καὶ Ἀρείῳ συνερράγη
_unresolved_facts.fix: Alexander Baucalis ... distinct from Alexander the bishop; Philostorgius says he held second rank and started the cause from which the quarrel between Alexander the bishop and Arius broke out. Note: The brief presents this as fact, but the source frames it as Philostorgius's report (φησι).

_unresolved_facts.claim: Constantius ... emperor in the upper Galatias, where the Alps are
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Κωνστάντιος, ὃ τοῦ μεγάλου Κωνσταντίνου πατήρ, ἀνδραγαθίαν τῶν ἄνω Γαλατιῶν, ἐν αἷς καὶ αἱ καλούμεναι Ἄλπεις, βασιλεὺς ἀπεδείχθη
_unresolved_facts.fix: Constantius ... was shown to be king/emperor because of manly virtue in the upper Galatias, among which are the so-called Alpeis. Note: The source says ἀνδραγαθίαν ('manly virtue/bravery') not that he was 'emperor in' the region; and Ἄλπεις/Alpeis is a place name within upper Galatia, not 'the Alps' in the modern sense. The brief's 'where the Alps are' is misleading.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Diocletian ... Emperor whose plot Constantine escaped
_unresolved_facts.fix: Diocletian ... Constantine escaped the plot of Diocletian. Note: The source says τὴν ἐπιβουλὴν ('the plot/ambush'), not specifically 'whose plot' in the sense of Diocletian personally plotting; the brief over-specifies.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Philostorgius assesses the books of Maccabees, Josephus, and Eusebius, then recounts the origin of the Arian dispute and the death of Constantine's father Constantius
_unresolved_facts.fix: Philostorgius assesses the books of Maccabees, Josephus, Phlegon, Dion, and Eusebius, then recounts the origin of the Arian dispute, the death of Constantine's father Constantius, and Constantine's conversion. Note: The brief omits Phlegon and Dion from the outline, and omits Constantine's conversion which follows Constantius's death in the source.
